newsitem.title: UK: Alcopop thirst set to ride out Chancellor's tax.
newsitem.headline: Alcopop thirst set to ride out Chancellor's tax.

text.p: Eight pence on a bottle of "alcopops" from January 1, put on by Chancellor Kenneth Clarke in his budget last month, is unlikely to quench the thirst for the latest fad among Britain's young drinkers, brewers say.
"We certainly believe it will withstand the increase," said Bob Cartwright, director of communications for Bass Taverns.

Alcopops, alcoholic versions of traditional soft drinks such as lemonade, have stormed ahead since brewer-to-leisure group Bass launched market leader Hoopers Hooch 18 months ago. Other brewers have scurried to launch their own alcopop faced with the runaway success of Hooch. Just 18 months ago Hooch and Two Dogs, owned by cider-maker Merrydown, were the only two competing brands but now there are more than 90.

"It's hardly desirable. But seven or eight pence on a bottle is not going to be drastic. We don't think eight pence is going to make any difference," said Merrydown group finance director Stephen Burke.

Hooch, which sells three million bottles a week, has captured around 200 million pounds ($331.4 million) of the 220 million-a-year alcopop market. Bass sold a staggering 320,000 barrels this year and that was during a relatively dull summer.
"It really took hold in the summer of 1995. The only problem we had was a shortage of supply. People seek it out in the pubs and it has developed very strong off-trade sales," said Cartwright.
SALE PREDICTED TO DOUBLE
Research company Datamonitor estimates total alcopop sales will double to 220 million pounds this year.

Some 65 percent of British alcopop sales come from alcoholic lemonades, largely driven by Hooch but future growth is expected to come from both alcoholic fruit carbonates, like orange or cherryade and also from alcholic sodas.

Hooch itself is now available in blackcurrant and Two Dogs has a variant called Rhubarb Rhubarb. In Britain sodas will be strong in niche markets like night-clubs, while fruit carbonates will keep their mass appeal, said Datamonitor.

But Britain's health lobby may still scupper the growing trend for alcopops. Organisations like Alcohol Concern continue to press government for a hefty tax increase and tighter controls on advertising and marketing.
Alcohol Concern wanted the Chancellor to slap on a 48 pence a bottle tax, taking an average alcopop to 1.50 pounds.

"We're still convinced that these drinks are being marketed in such a way that they are intended to appeal to under age drinkers. A lot of the damage has already been done because they have established a presence with under age drinkers," said Alcohol Concern press officer Lee Lixenberg.
Only four of Alcohol Concern's 21 complaints were upheld by the Portman Group, a body funded by seven leading brewers and distillers to promote sensible drinking.
Among those rejected were its complaints against the marketing of brands Ravers and Love Byte.
The Portman Group upheld complaints that some "alcopops" marketing targeted drinkers under the legal limit of 18.
As a result Bass agreed to remove its smiling fruit image from its "Hoopers Hooch" brand while Whitbread agreed to change the name of its Lemon Jag and Vanilla Heist alcopops.
The industry body also persuaded Spilt Drinks to remove a cartoon character from its Jammin' brand.
Carlsberg-Tetley, whose alcopops include Lemonhead and Orangehead, escaped criticism.
The drinks companies themselves say alcopops are aimed at 18 to 24 year olds and that anyhow it is for shopkeepers and supermarkets to uphold the law.
BATTLE SET TO CONTINUE
But the battle between the drinks industry and health organisations is likely to rumble on as each side points to its own body of survey's as evidence of its argument.
A survey done by Off-License News in September showed 68 percent of 50 Police Licensing Officers thought alcopops had become the favourite tipple of under 18 year olds.
A recent survey of more than 1,000 children aged 11 to 15 by The Business Media Group when asked "what drinks are in" showed alcopops second to Coca-Cola.

But when 600 15 to 17 year olds were asked in a survey by the Scottish Council on Alcohol what they drink alcopops came a poor fifth to cider, spirits and wine on the basis that it was too expensive and not strong enough. ($1=.6056 Pence)
